title: Key Ideas and Details
summary: Main idea, details, sequence, cause–effect, comparisons and inferences on ACT Reading, with worked examples, trap analysis and a full literary narrative practice passage.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Key Ideas and Details is the **largest category on ACT Reading: 44–52% of the scored questions**. With 27 scored questions, that is roughly 12 to 14 questions on every test. These questions check whether you understood **what the passage says** and **what it clearly means**. They appear in every passage type, including the literary narrative (fiction or memoir) that is always one of the three scored passages.

rows: Main idea / central idea
"The passage mainly focuses on:" / "The main idea of paragraph 4 is that:"
Summarize the whole passage (or paragraph) in one sentence
Detail
"According to the passage, …" / "The narrator states that …"
Find the sentence; the answer is a paraphrase of it
Sequence
"Which of the following events happens first?"
Put events in TIME order, not reading order
Cause–effect
"According to the passage, X happened because:"
Find the reason the text gives (because, so, since, as a result)
Comparison
"Compared with A, B is described as:"
Find the description of BOTH things and compare
Inference
"It can most reasonably be inferred that …" / "The narrator's statement most strongly suggests …"
Take ONE small step beyond the words, never two

blocks.text: The method, step by step

items: **Read the blurb and know who the narrator is.** In literary passages, ask: Who is telling the story? Is he a child in the story or an adult looking back? Many Key Ideas questions depend on this.

**Track the plot as you read.** For a narrative, your 3-word map becomes a short timeline: [1] sent to uncle, [2] sweeps 3 weeks, [3] watches, [4] gets wheel, [5] fails, [6] note, [7] succeeds, [8] pen, [9] adult lesson.
**Find the line before you choose.** For every detail, cause–effect or comparison question, go to the paragraph and read the sentence before, the sentence and the sentence after.
**Predict in your own words.** Write a 3–6-word answer on your scrap paper before looking at the choices.
**Match meaning, not words.** The right answer usually paraphrases the text. A choice that copies the passage's exact words but changes one relationship (cause, order, comparison) is a classic trap.
**For inferences, test the step.** Ask: "Does the text make this almost certain?" If you need to imagine extra facts, eliminate it.
**For main-idea questions, check the ends.** The correct choice fits both the beginning and the end of the passage; in memoir, the end often reveals the meaning.

blocks.title: الـ Inference يعني خطوة واحدة بس
blocks.text: الاستنتاج في الـ ACT مش تخمين. الإجابة الصح بتبقى قريبة جدًا من الكلام المكتوب، خطوة واحدة بعده. لو لقيت نفسك بتقول «ممكن يكون علشان…» وبتضيف حاجات مش في القطعة، يبقى الاختيار ده غلط.
Sequence, cause–effect and comparison: the three relationship questions
Many wrong answers on Key Ideas questions contain true facts from the passage but connect them the wrong way. Learn to check the **relationship**, not just the facts.

rows: Sequence (time)
then, later, by March, the next day, before, after, years later, now
Reading order ≠ time order: memoirs often start in the present and flash back
Cause–effect
because, so, since, as a result, that is why, which made
Reversed cause and effect: the effect is offered as the cause
Comparison
like, unlike, more than, nothing like, instead of, while
Half-right: one side of the comparison is correct, the other is invented

blocks.text: Worked examples
Read this short memoir excerpt (shorter than a real ACT passage, so we can focus on the method). Then study each question, the answer, and why each wrong choice is wrong.

[1] We moved to Cairo in January, in the middle of the school year, which my mother said was the worst possible time and my father said was the only possible time. On my first morning at the new school, the teacher placed me at a desk beside a boy named Tarek, who looked at my old-fashioned pencil case and said nothing at all.

[2] For a week, Tarek and I shared the desk like two strangers sharing a bus seat. Then, during a mathematics lesson, he dropped his ruler, and I picked it up before he could. He looked surprised. The next day, a small bag of sunflower seeds appeared on my side of the desk. Neither of us mentioned it.

[3] By March we were walking home together. I learned later that Tarek had also arrived in the middle of a school year, two years before me, and that nobody had picked up anything for him.
**Worked example 1 — main idea**
**Question:** The excerpt mainly focuses on:

items: A) the narrator's difficult relationship with his new teacher.
B) a friendship that grows slowly from a small act of kindness.
C) the disagreement between the narrator's parents about moving.
D) the problems of changing schools in the middle of the year.

blocks.text: **Answer: B.** The excerpt moves from silence (paragraph 1) to a small kindness and a gift (paragraph 2) to walking home together (paragraph 3). B covers all three paragraphs.

items: **A is wrong** — Off-topic: the teacher appears only once, to seat the narrator.
**C is wrong** — Too narrow: the parents' disagreement is one sentence of background.
**D is wrong** — Too broad: the excerpt is about one friendship, not the general problems of changing schools.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — sequence**
**Question:** Which event happened immediately before the bag of sunflower seeds appeared on the narrator's side of the desk?

items: A) The teacher seated the narrator beside Tarek.
B) The narrator learned about Tarek's own arrival at the school.
C) The narrator picked up Tarek's ruler.
D) The two boys began walking home together.

blocks.text: **Answer: C.** Paragraph 2: the ruler is picked up "during a mathematics lesson", and "the next day" the seeds appear. Look for the time signal: "the next day" links the two events directly.

items: **A is wrong** — Happened before, but not immediately before: a week passed in between.
**B is wrong** — Happened much later ("I learned later") — the trap of reading order vs time order.
**D is wrong** — Happened afterwards, "by March".

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — comparison**
**Question:** The narrator's parents differed in their views of the January move in that:

items: A) his mother thought it was badly timed, while his father thought there was no other choice.
B) his mother wanted to move to Cairo, while his father did not.
C) both parents thought it was the best possible time to move.
D) his father worried about the new school, while his mother worried about the city.

blocks.text: **Answer: A.** "My mother said was the worst possible time and my father said was the only possible time." Only possible = there was no other choice. A states both sides correctly.

items: **B is wrong** — Not stated: the text gives their views of the timing, not of Cairo itself.
**C is wrong** — Reversed for the mother and not true for the father: "only possible" is not "best".
**D is wrong** — Invented: neither worry is mentioned (outside-the-text trap).

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — inference**
**Question:** The last sentence of the excerpt most strongly suggests that Tarek:

items: A) disliked all new students until the narrator arrived.
B) had been lonely when he first arrived and valued the narrator's small kindness.
C) had told the teacher to seat the narrator beside him.
D) had dropped his ruler on purpose to test the narrator.

blocks.text: **Answer: B.** Tarek also arrived mid-year and "nobody had picked up anything for him." One small step: he knew how it felt to be ignored, which explains his surprise and his gift.

items: **A is wrong** — Too extreme: "all new students" goes far beyond the text.
**C is wrong** — Two steps away: nothing suggests Tarek spoke to the teacher.
**D is wrong** — Pure speculation: the passage says only that he "dropped his ruler"; inventing a motive is not inference.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Right words, wrong relationship.** The choice uses the passage's own words but reverses cause and effect or changes the order of events.
**Reading order vs time order.** Memoirs jump between the past and the present; build a timeline before answering sequence questions.
**Half-right comparisons.** Check BOTH halves of a comparison choice against the text.
**Over-inference.** "Most reasonably inferred" means one small step. Extreme words (all, never, completely, always) usually signal two steps too many.
**Main idea = favourite detail.** In fiction, students often choose the most exciting moment. The main idea must include the ending and the meaning.
**Confusing the narrator with the author, or the young narrator with the adult narrator.** "I am a structural engineer now" is the older narrator looking back; his feelings then and now may differ.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: For literary narrative: identify the narrator, the time frame, and the turning point while you read.
Detail and cause–effect questions: go back to the line every time; never answer from memory.
Predict a short answer before reading the choices.
Sequence: number the events 1–4 on your scrap paper using the time signals.
Inference: choose the most cautious choice that the text strongly supports.

blocks.title: القطعة الأدبية
blocks.text: في الـ literary narrative اسأل نفسك 3 أسئلة وإنت بتقرا: مين اللي بيحكي؟ بيحكي وهو صغير ولا وهو كبير بيفتكر؟ وإيه اللحظة اللي غيرت القصة؟ أغلب أسئلة الـ main idea والـ inference إجابتها في آخر باراجراف.
Practice

Now try a full literary narrative passage (about 750 words) with 9 Key Ideas and Details questions. It is **untimed**, but aim for about 10 minutes. Build a timeline as you read, and go back to the text for every answer.

blocks.title: ACT Reading practice — Literary Narrative passage
blocks.intro: One passage, 9 questions, untimed. Track the narrator and the order of events, predict before you look at the choices, and keep inferences to one small step.

questions.p:
LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is adapted from a short story. The narrator remembers a summer he spent working in his uncle's bicycle shop.

[1] The summer I turned fifteen, my father decided that I had spent enough afternoons asleep in front of the television, and he sent me to work for his older brother, Uncle Fathy, who repaired bicycles in a narrow shop two streets from the sea. I did not want to go. My cousin Karim had worked there the year before and had come home every evening with black hands and stories about how Uncle Fathy never said more than ten words in a day. "He'll make you sweep for a month," Karim warned me. "Then, if you're lucky, he'll let you sweep for another month."

[2] Karim was wrong about one thing: I swept for only three weeks. Every morning I arrived at eight, rolled up the metal shutter, and pushed a broom across the concrete floor while my uncle sat on an upturned crate drinking tea and reading the newspaper. He did not tell me to work harder or more slowly. He did not tell me anything. When I finished, he would look at the floor, look at me, and nod once, and that was the only sign that I existed.

[3] What I did during those weeks, without meaning to, was watch. I watched him lift a bicycle onto the stand with one hand, spin the back wheel, and listen to it the way a doctor listens to a chest. I watched him find, by touch alone, the single loose spoke among thirty-six. I watched customers arrive angry about a squeaking chain and leave ten minutes later, almost embarrassed by how little the repair had cost. By the end of the third week, I could have told you which tool he would reach for before his hand moved.

[4] On the first day of the fourth week, he handed me a wheel instead of the broom. It belonged to a boy's bicycle and was so badly bent that it wobbled like a plate about to slide off a table. My uncle set a spoke key in my palm, pointed at the wheel, and went back to his newspaper.

[5] I spent the whole morning on that wheel. I tightened spokes that should have been loosened and loosened ones that should have been tightened, always by a full turn or more, and by noon the wobble was worse than when I had started. Twice I looked up, hoping he would rescue me; twice he turned a page. At lunch I ate my bread and cheese outside on the step, close to tears, sure that Karim had been right about everything and that I would be sent home in disgrace.

[6] When I came back in, the wheel was exactly where I had left it. My uncle had not fixed it for me. But on the bench beside it, in his slow, square handwriting, there was a scrap of paper with a small drawing—a circle with an arrow pointing to one side of it—and two words: "Small turns."

[7] I began again. This time I turned each spoke a quarter-turn at most, spun the wheel, watched where it touched the brake pad, and turned again. It was dull, careful work, nothing like the confident movements I had admired from beside the broom. Late in the afternoon, the wheel spun in a straight, quiet circle, and I sat back so suddenly that I nearly knocked over the stand.

[8] My uncle folded his newspaper, came over, and spun the wheel himself. He watched it for what felt like a full minute. Then he took a repair tag from the drawer, the kind he tied to every finished bicycle, and instead of writing his own name on it, he held out the pen to me.

[9] I am a structural engineer now, and I have spent my working life on projects far larger than a child's bicycle. Yet whenever a calculation goes wrong and I feel the old urge to make one big correction and be done with it, I think of that scrap of paper. I kept it in my wallet for years, until it fell apart. I never asked my uncle why he wrote the note instead of simply showing me. I think I understand now that showing me would have fixed the wheel, while writing it fixed something else.
c: a frustrating day of work through which the narrator learned a lesson that stayed with him as an adult.
the narrator's long competition with his cousin Karim over who was the better worker.
the history of Uncle Fathy's bicycle shop and the customers who used it.
the reasons the narrator later chose to become a structural engineer.
questions.e: The story builds to the wheel and the note (paragraphs 4–8), and paragraph 9 shows the lesson lasting into adulthood. B is not in the text (no competition); C is too narrow and off-focus; D is reversed in emphasis: the passage never explains WHY he became an engineer.

questions.q: According to the narrator, Karim's prediction turned out to be wrong because the narrator:
c: was given more interesting work than Karim had been.
was never asked to sweep the shop at all.
swept the shop for less time than Karim had said he would.
found that his uncle talked much more than Karim had claimed.
questions.e: Paragraph 2: "Karim was wrong about one thing: I swept for only three weeks," while Karim had predicted a month or two. A is not stated (we never learn what Karim did); B is contradicted; D is reversed: the uncle "did not tell me anything."

questions.q: Which of the following events happens first in the passage?
c: The narrator eats lunch outside on the step.
The narrator finds a note on the bench.
The uncle holds out a pen to the narrator.
The narrator can predict which tool his uncle will use.
questions.e: Order: end of the third week (he can predict the tools, paragraph 3) → the wheel (paragraph 4) → lunch on the step (paragraph 5) → the note (paragraph 6) → the pen (paragraph 8). The trap is choosing the first event you READ about in the wheel story instead of the earliest event in time.

questions.q: According to paragraph 5, the wobble in the wheel became worse during the morning because the narrator:
c: used a tool that was the wrong size for the wheel.
made large adjustments to the wrong spokes.
refused to follow his uncle's spoken instructions.
worked too slowly and stopped too often to look up.
questions.e: He "tightened spokes that should have been loosened and loosened ones that should have been tightened, always by a full turn or more." A is never mentioned; C is impossible (the uncle gave no spoken instructions); D is reversed: the problem was big, fast turns, not slowness.

questions.q: Compared with the way his uncle worked in paragraph 3, the narrator's work in paragraph 7 is described as:
c: faster and more confident.
just as skilful but less interesting to watch.
slower, duller and more cautious.
careless at first but quickly impressive.
questions.e: Paragraph 7 calls it "dull, careful work, nothing like the confident movements I had admired." A is reversed. B is half-right: "less interesting" fits, but "just as skilful" is not supported. D describes the morning (paragraph 5), not paragraph 7 (wrong place).

questions.p:
LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is adapted from a short story. The narrator remembers a summer he spent working in his uncle's bicycle shop.

[1] The summer I turned fifteen, my father decided that I had spent enough afternoons asleep in front of the television, and he sent me to work for his older brother, Uncle Fathy, who repaired bicycles in a narrow shop two streets from the sea. I did not want to go. My cousin Karim had worked there the year before and had come home every evening with black hands and stories about how Uncle Fathy never said more than ten words in a day. "He'll make you sweep for a month," Karim warned me. "Then, if you're lucky, he'll let you sweep for another month."

[2] Karim was wrong about one thing: I swept for only three weeks. Every morning I arrived at eight, rolled up the metal shutter, and pushed a broom across the concrete floor while my uncle sat on an upturned crate drinking tea and reading the newspaper. He did not tell me to work harder or more slowly. He did not tell me anything. When I finished, he would look at the floor, look at me, and nod once, and that was the only sign that I existed.

[3] What I did during those weeks, without meaning to, was watch. I watched him lift a bicycle onto the stand with one hand, spin the back wheel, and listen to it the way a doctor listens to a chest. I watched him find, by touch alone, the single loose spoke among thirty-six. I watched customers arrive angry about a squeaking chain and leave ten minutes later, almost embarrassed by how little the repair had cost. By the end of the third week, I could have told you which tool he would reach for before his hand moved.

[4] On the first day of the fourth week, he handed me a wheel instead of the broom. It belonged to a boy's bicycle and was so badly bent that it wobbled like a plate about to slide off a table. My uncle set a spoke key in my palm, pointed at the wheel, and went back to his newspaper.

[5] I spent the whole morning on that wheel. I tightened spokes that should have been loosened and loosened ones that should have been tightened, always by a full turn or more, and by noon the wobble was worse than when I had started. Twice I looked up, hoping he would rescue me; twice he turned a page. At lunch I ate my bread and cheese outside on the step, close to tears, sure that Karim had been right about everything and that I would be sent home in disgrace.

[6] When I came back in, the wheel was exactly where I had left it. My uncle had not fixed it for me. But on the bench beside it, in his slow, square handwriting, there was a scrap of paper with a small drawing—a circle with an arrow pointing to one side of it—and two words: "Small turns."

[7] I began again. This time I turned each spoke a quarter-turn at most, spun the wheel, watched where it touched the brake pad, and turned again. It was dull, careful work, nothing like the confident movements I had admired from beside the broom. Late in the afternoon, the wheel spun in a straight, quiet circle, and I sat back so suddenly that I nearly knocked over the stand.

[8] My uncle folded his newspaper, came over, and spun the wheel himself. He watched it for what felt like a full minute. Then he took a repair tag from the drawer, the kind he tied to every finished bicycle, and instead of writing his own name on it, he held out the pen to me.

[9] I am a structural engineer now, and I have spent my working life on projects far larger than a child's bicycle. Yet whenever a calculation goes wrong and I feel the old urge to make one big correction and be done with it, I think of that scrap of paper. I kept it in my wallet for years, until it fell apart. I never asked my uncle why he wrote the note instead of simply showing me. I think I understand now that showing me would have fixed the wheel, while writing it fixed something else.
questions.q: The narrator's statement that the nod "was the only sign that I existed" (paragraph 2) most strongly suggests that during his first weeks he felt:
c: largely ignored by his uncle.
proud that his uncle praised his sweeping.
angry enough to consider leaving the shop.
confident that he would soon be repairing bicycles.
questions.e: "The only sign that I existed" is an exaggeration that shows how little attention he received. B is too strong: a nod is not praise. C goes too far (outside the text: he never thinks of leaving at this point). D has no support in paragraph 2.

questions.q: When the uncle holds out the pen instead of writing his own name on the repair tag (paragraph 8), he is most likely showing that he:
c: wants the narrator to practise his handwriting.
is too tired to write after watching the wheel.
plans to give the narrator his own shop.

questions.e: The uncle "tied [a tag] to every finished bicycle" with his own name; giving the pen means this finished repair belongs to the narrator. A and B are literal readings with no support; C is far too extreme.

questions.q: According to paragraph 9, what did the narrator do with the scrap of paper?
c: He gave it back to his uncle at the end of the summer.
He kept it in his wallet until it fell apart.
He framed it and hung it in his office.
He showed it to his cousin Karim as proof of his success.
questions.e: Paragraph 9: "I kept it in my wallet for years, until it fell apart." The other choices are invented details; on detail questions, only words the passage actually states can be correct.

questions.q: In the final sentence of the passage, the narrator suggests that his uncle's note:
c: repaired the wheel more quickly than a demonstration would have.
showed that his uncle was unable to explain the repair in words.
taught him a careful way of solving problems on his own.

items: Key Ideas and Details = 44–52% of scored ACT Reading questions — the biggest category.
Every detail answer is a paraphrase of a sentence you can point to.
Check the relationship: time order, cause–effect and comparison traps use true facts connected the wrong way.
An inference is one small, safe step beyond the text, never a guess.
In literary narrative, know who is telling the story and from what point in time.
